title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Princess Mary arrived in Moscow after her meeting with Rostov. There she found her nephew with his tutor, and a letter from Prince Andrew with instructions for reaching her Aunt Malvintseva at Voronezh. A feeling like temptation had tormented her during her father's illness, and since his death, and above all since meeting Rostov. Now it was smothered by preparations for the journey, worry about her brother, settling into a new house, meeting new people and looking after her nephew's education. She was sad. After a month in quiet surroundings, she felt her father's loss more and more deeply, and in her mind it was tied to the ruin of Russia. She was agitated and ceaselessly tormented by the thought of the dangers her brother, the one intimate person she had left, was facing. She worried, too, about her nephew's education, for which she had always felt herself unfit. Yet in the depths of her soul she felt at peace, a peace that came from knowing she had stifled the personal dreams and hopes that had been about to awaken in her, those linked to her meeting with Rostov.

The day after her party, the governor's wife came to see Malvintseva and talked over her plan with the aunt. She remarked that a formal betrothal was of course not to be thought of in the present circumstances, but the young people could still be brought together to get to know one another. Malvintseva agreed, and the governor's wife began talking about Rostov in Mary's presence, praising him and telling how he had blushed when Princess Mary's name came up. But Princess Mary felt pain rather than joy. Her peace of mind was gone, and desires, doubts, self-reproach and hopes woke up again.

In the two days before Rostov called, Princess Mary kept wondering how she should behave with him. First she decided not to come into the drawing room when he visited her aunt, since it would not be proper to receive visitors in her deep mourning. Then she thought that would be rude after what he had done for her. Next it struck her that her aunt and the governor's wife had designs on her and Rostov, as their looks and words at times seemed to confirm. Then she told herself that only she, with her sinful nature, could think this of them: they could not forget that, in her situation, still in deep mourning, such matchmaking would insult her and her father's memory. If she did go down to see him, Princess Mary pictured the words he would say to her and the words she would say to him. At times those words seemed undeservedly cold, and at times they seemed to mean too much. Above all she feared that the confusion she felt would overwhelm her and betray her the moment she saw him.

But on Sunday after church, when the footman announced in the drawing room that Count Rostov had called, the princess showed no confusion. Only a slight blush spread over her cheeks, and her eyes lit up with a new, radiant light.
"You have met him, Aunt?" she said in a calm voice, unable to understand herself how she could seem so calm and natural.

Rostov came into the room, and the princess dropped her eyes for an instant, as if to give the visitor time to greet her aunt. Then, just as Nicholas turned to her, she lifted her head and met his gaze with shining eyes. With a movement full of dignity and grace she half rose, smiling with pleasure, held out her slender, delicate hand and began to speak, in a voice where deep new womanly notes sounded for the first time. Mademoiselle Bourienne, who was in the drawing room, stared at Princess Mary in bewildered surprise. She was a consummate coquette herself, and she could not have done better when meeting a man she wanted to attract.
"Either black suits her particularly well, or she has really improved a great deal without my noticing. And above all, what tact and grace!" thought Mademoiselle Bourienne.

Had Princess Mary been able to reflect at that moment, the change in herself would have surprised her even more than it surprised Mademoiselle Bourienne. From the instant she recognized that dear, loved face, a new life force seized her and made her speak and act independently of her own will. Her face was suddenly transformed from the moment Rostov entered. It was as if a light had been kindled inside a carved and painted lantern, so that the intricate, skillful, artistic work on its sides, which had looked dark, coarse and meaningless before, was suddenly shown in unexpected and striking beauty. For the first time, all the pure, spiritual, inward travail she had lived through came to the surface. All her inward labor, her dissatisfaction with herself, her sufferings, her strivings after goodness, her meekness, love and self-sacrifice — all this now shone in those radiant eyes, in her delicate smile, and in every trait of her gentle face.
Rostov saw all this as clearly as if he had known her whole life. He felt that the being before him was quite different from anyone he had met, and better, and above all better than himself.

Their conversation was very simple and unimportant. They talked about the war and, like everyone else, unconsciously exaggerated their sorrow over it. They talked about their last meeting, with Nicholas trying to change the subject. They talked about the governor's kind wife, about Nicholas' relatives, and about Princess Mary's.

She did not talk about her brother, and she steered the conversation away as soon as her aunt mentioned Andrew. She could evidently speak of Russia's misfortunes with a certain artificiality, but her brother was too close to her heart, and she neither could nor would speak lightly about him. Nicholas noticed this, as he noticed every shade of Princess Mary's character with an attention unusual for him, and everything confirmed his belief that she was a quite unusual and extraordinary being. Nicholas blushed and was flustered when people spoke to him about the princess (as she did when he was mentioned), and even when he merely thought of her. But in her presence he felt quite at ease, and he said not at all what he had prepared, but whatever came to him at the moment, and it was quite fitting.

When a pause came during his short visit, Nicholas did what people usually do when there are children. He turned to Prince Andrew's little son, caressed him and asked whether he would like to be a hussar. He took the boy on his knee, played with him, and looked around at Princess Mary. With a softened, happy, timid look, she watched the boy she loved in the arms of the man she loved. Nicholas noticed that look too and, as if he understood it, flushed with pleasure and began kissing the boy with good-natured playfulness.

Princess Mary was in mourning and did not go out into society, and Nicholas did not think it right to call on her again. Still, the governor's wife went on with her matchmaking. She told Nicholas the flattering things Princess Mary said about him, and told Princess Mary the flattering things he said about her, and she insisted that he declare himself to Princess Mary. To that end she arranged a meeting between the young people at the bishop's house before Mass.
Rostov told the governor's wife that he would not make any declaration to Princess Mary, but he promised to go.

At Tilsit, Rostov had not let himself doubt that what everybody considered right was right, and it was the same now. After a short but sincere struggle between his wish to run his life by his own sense of justice and the pull of obedient submission to circumstances, he chose the latter. He yielded to the power he felt carrying him irresistibly, he knew not where. He knew that, after his promise to Sonya, declaring his feelings to Princess Mary would be, in his own judgment, base. And he knew that he would never act basely. But he also knew (or rather felt, at the bottom of his heart) that by giving in now to the force of circumstances and to those who were guiding him, he was not only doing nothing wrong but doing something very important, more important than anything he had ever done in his life.

After meeting Princess Mary, the course of his life went on outwardly as before, but all his old amusements lost their charm and he often thought about her. Yet he never thought about her as he had thought about every young lady he had met in society, or as he had for a long time, and at one point rapturously, thought about Sonya. Like almost all honest-hearted young men, he had pictured each of those young ladies as a possible wife and fitted her in his imagination to all the conditions of married life: a white dressing gown, his wife at the tea table, his wife's carriage, little ones, Mamma and Papa, how they got on with her, and so on. These pictures of the future had pleased him. But with Princess Mary, to whom they were trying to get him engaged, he could never picture any future married life. When he tried, the pictures looked incongruous and false. It frightened him.
